title: Design Kafka — Replication
description: Deep dive into Kafka's replication protocol: ISR mechanics, min.insync.replicas, unclean leader election, idempotent producers, and transactional exactly-once semantics.

segments.text: Kafka stores data on disk, but disks fail. Replication ensures that when a broker dies, no messages are lost. But replication introduces consistency challenges. The ISR — in-sync replica set — is Kafka's solution, and understanding it is essential for any Staff-level design discussion involving Kafka.

The ISR is the set of replicas that are caught up with the leader. A follower stays in the ISR as long as it replicates within replica.lag.time.max.ms — default ten seconds. If a follower falls behind, it's removed from the ISR. When the leader receives a write with acks-all, it only waits for ISR members to acknowledge.

min.insync.replicas is your durability guarantee. Set it to two with a replication factor of three, and acks-all requires at least two replicas to acknowledge. If two replicas are down, the partition becomes unavailable for writes — better than losing data. LinkedIn runs min.insync.replicas equals two for all critical topics.

When the leader fails, a new leader is elected from the ISR. This is clean leader election — no data loss because ISR members have all committed messages. But what if all ISR members are down? Unclean leader election allows a non-ISR replica to become leader — it has data, but it's missing recent messages. You choose: availability or data loss.

Your Kafka cluster has replication factor three. Two brokers hosting replicas of a critical partition fail simultaneously. The remaining replica is out of sync by five minutes of data. Do you enable unclean leader election?
segments.thought_prompt: Unclean leader election: accept 5 minutes of data loss for availability, or wait for ISR recovery?

segments.text: The idempotent producer prevents duplicate writes. Each producer instance gets a Producer ID from the broker. Each message gets a monotonically increasing sequence number. If the broker receives a message with a PID and sequence it's already seen, it deduplicates silently. This is transparent — just set enable.idempotence equals true.

Kafka transactions enable exactly-once across topics. A producer starts a transaction, writes to multiple partitions, and commits atomically. Either all writes are visible to consumers or none are. This is built on a transaction coordinator and a transaction log — similar to two-phase commit but optimized for Kafka's log-based architecture.

The read-process-write pattern is Kafka's exactly-once consumer. Read from input topic, process, write to output topic, and commit the input offset — all in one transaction. If any step fails, the entire transaction is aborted. The consumer offset and output messages are committed atomically. Kafka Streams uses this internally.

Transactions have a cost. The transaction coordinator adds latency — roughly ten to twenty milliseconds per transaction commit. To amortize this, batch multiple messages per transaction. Confluent recommends committing every one hundred milliseconds or every hundred messages, whichever comes first. This balances exactly-once guarantees with throughput.

You're designing a financial event streaming system. Events must never be duplicated, never lost, and processed in order. What combination of Kafka producer, broker, and consumer settings achieves this?
segments.thought_prompt: Configure Kafka end-to-end for financial events: no duplicates, no loss, in-order processing.

segments.text: Kafka replication is a carefully designed system of tradeoffs. ISR tracks caught-up replicas, min.insync.replicas sets your durability floor, clean leader election prevents data loss, idempotent producers eliminate duplicates, and transactions provide atomic multi-partition writes. The complete recipe for exactly-once: idempotent producer plus transactional read-process-write pattern.
